title: Surgical and intravital microscopy protocol to image Trypanosoma brucei-host interactions in live rodent models
protocol: Inject mice with antibodies against specific endothelial receptors you aim to block.
Determine the duration of blocking antibody lifetime in mice.
Calculate antibody affinity and receptor turnover rate for each receptor of interest.
Ensure maximum blocking at correct time windows.
Dilute blocking antibodies to desired concentration.
Calculate volume needed per mouse.
Secure mice in restrainer for intravenous injection.
Inject 20–30 μg of blocking antibodies per mouse daily over a course of 6 days.
Infect C57BL/6J mice with Trypanosoma brucei by intraperitoneal or intradermal injection.
Perform infection timing between 24–25 hours after antibody injection.
Thaw a blood stabilate from liquid nitrogen or -80°C storage.
Centrifuge the stabilate for 2 minutes at 800 g.
Remove all supernatant to remove glycerol.
Resuspend in 10 mL of HMI-11 complete media.
Recover for 24 hours at 37°C in 5% CO2.
Count parasites using a suitable method.
Dilute parasites to have 2000 parasites/200 μL volume.
Inject 200 μL intraperitoneally into C57BL/6J mice.
Thaw a stabilate of T. brucei blood trypomastigotes.
Place thawed cells in HMI-11 culture media for at least 24 hours.
Centrifuge cells at 800 g for 1 minute to remove glycerol.
Resuspend cells in 5–10 mL of HMI-11 media.
Transfer resuspended cells into a 75 mm² flask.
Incubate the flask at 37°C with 5% CO₂.
Observe T. brucei parasites under the microscope after 24 hours.
Assess the motility and general morphology of the parasites to determine their suitability for infection.
Dilute or concentrate parasites as necessary to have 2 × 10^3 parasites per mouse in HMI-11 volume required for 200 μL injection (i.e., 10^4 parasites/mL).
Resuspend parasites in HMI-11 to prepare a suspension containing 2 × 10^3 parasites per 200 μL.
Load an insulin syringe with 200 μL of HMI-11 + T. brucei for injection into C57BL/6 mice by intraperitoneal or intradermal injection.
Anesthetize mice before surgical procedures and IVM.

Prepare ketamine/xylazine solution in a sterile Falcon tube by adding 0.8 mL xylazine (20 mg/mL) and 1.2 mL ketamine (100 mg/mL), then add 8 mL pharmaceutical grade distilled water or sterile 0.9% NaCl to obtain 10 mL of anesthetic solution.
Weigh mice before administering anesthetic mixture, giving 100 μL per 10 g body weight (i.e., 120 mg/kg ketamine + 16 mg/kg xylazine) via intraperitoneal injection.
Place the animal back in its cage until it is immobilized (confirm loss of upright reflex).
Avoid stressing the animal while holding or manipulating it.
Prepare additional aliquots of anesthetic for surgery and imaging sites.
Monitor anesthetic depth by checking the pedal withdrawal reflex.
Turn on microscope including all lasers to be used.
Turn on incubation system to 27°C–30°C if the microscope contains a temperature-controlled chamber.
Otherwise, turn on heating mat to 27°C–30°C.
Prepare all settings in hardware and software before starting surgeries.
Ensure body temperature is maintained during anesthesia in mice.
Perform surgeries for intravital microscopy immediately prior to imaging.
Monitor anesthetic effects and provide additional doses as needed during long procedures.
Maintain hydration and integrity of the tissue throughout the imaging procedure.
Check for righting reflex by placing the mouse in a dorsal position and observing its ability to return to the ventral position.
Proceed to check for pedal withdrawal reflex once the righting reflex is absent, pinching the metacarpal region of each hind foot with index and thumb or blunt forceps (avoid injuring the mouse).
Proceed to surgery only when both hind feet lack the pedal withdrawal reflex.
Protect the mouse’s eyes from drying using specialized gel.
Clean the mouse hair and skin with 70% ethanol at the site of surgical incision.
Observe under microscope to remove any potential hair before imaging.
Remove any remaining individual hairs using forceps or a moist cotton swab.
Place the mouse in ventral recumbency for brain intravital microscopy (IVM).
Perform a surgical incision on the mouse scalp to expose the region of interest in the skull and brain.
Expose the region of interest by extending the incision from the olfactory bulb to the posterior region of the head.
Inject anesthetic intraperitoneally.
Prepare surgical site by making an incision as shown in the diagram.
Optionally thin skull using a surgical drill, leaving meninges intact.
Alternatively remove skull cap to expose brain directly for imaging.
Place window for imaging on exposed tissue without a coverslip.
Optionally place a round coverslip using surgical glue over the tissue.
Optionally attach a round coverslip with a vacuum ring on top of the incision.
Secure mouse head in stereotaxic instrument at three points: teeth and both ears.
Support mouse chin to aid immobilization during imaging.
Add dyes intravenously before securing mouse for imaging if required by experimental conditions.
Use an upright microscope to image brain, with objective reaching from above.
Imaging can be performed through the skull without further surgical procedure.
Skull thinning can be performed using a spherical surgical drill at 30,000 rpm until remaining skull thickness is 10–20 μm.
Measure the thickness of the thinned skull by second harmonic generation.
A surgical incision to remove a piece of the skull can be made using a surgical drill and instruments carefully to avoid brain damage.
Place a window to reduce brain swelling for short-term imaging up to 2 hours.
Verify that no hair is present on the area of interest before proceeding with imaging or placing a window.
If not required, use immersion oil directly on the intact or thinned skull for imaging.
Cover the surgical site with a hydration solution or 1× PBS if a window is not needed.
Add surgical glue around the contour of the incision to place a coverslip on the site of interest.
Secure a coverslip on a holder attached to a vacuum pump and place it over the surgical site.
Apply 20–25 mmHg of reversible vacuum to allow loose adherence of the coverslip to the brain surface.
Place the mouse on the imaging stage.
Immobilize the mouse's head using a stereotaxic instrument that supports both ears and the front of the head, e.g., via the teeth.
Inject dyes or conjugated antibodies into the mouse for imaging.
Position an upright microscope with at least a 63× objective over the site of surgical incision.
Acquire images to confirm no significant vascular damage or alterations in blood flow.
Place the mouse in ventral recumbency.
Make a surgical incision immediately below the neck and skull, extending slightly above the shoulder blades to visualize the isc-BAT.
Inject anesthetic intraperitoneally.
Generate a small cut between the neck and the shoulder blades to find the interscapular brown adipose tissue.
Place window for imaging.
Secure mouse head using a stereotaxic instrument securing teeth, and both ears.
Add dyes intravenously if required.
Place mouse in ventral recumbency for surgery.
Immobilize mouse head using a stereotaxic instrument that supports both ears and the front of the head.
Inject dyes or conjugated antibodies of interest into the mouse.
Use an upright microscope with at least a 63× objective, positioned at the site of the surgical incision.
Confirm that no significant vascular damage or blood flow alterations occurred.
Acquire images as needed.
Inject 70 kDa FITC-Dextran, Hoechst, and TdTom AnTat1.1E T. brucei into the isc-BAT at day 5 post-infection.
Perform lung IVM procedure.
Timing for lung IVM is 20–30 minutes.
Place the mouse in the dorsal recumbency.
Prepare the surgical site.
(Optional) Perform assisted ventilation using a nose cone or endotracheal intubation and link to a ventilator.
Inject anesthetic intraperitoneally.
Perform a tracheotomy to intubate mice for assisted ventilation.
Incise the chest cavity with a thoracotomy of 0.5 cm–1 cm wide on the left side of the chest.
Resect up to 3 ribs around the 5th rib during thoracotomy.
Stabilize the incision site using rib retractors.
Place window for imaging using a suction system linked to a ring that acts as a holder for a glass slide.
Create a vacuum leading to stabilization of the lung.
Use a round coverslip (#1.5, 15–20 mm diameter) to make a window allowing loose adherence to the lung surface via 20–25 mmHg of reversible vacuum.
Place mouse on stage in dorsal recumbency for imaging.
Immobobilize all limbs and tail with adhesive tape.
Introduce tubing for oxygenation and for vacuum generation to the setup on the microscope stage.
Position an inverted microscope objective at least 63× over the site of the optical window.
Confirm no significant vascular damage or blood flow alterations occurred, then acquire images as needed.
Place the mouse in the dorsal recumbency.
Perform assisted ventilation using endotracheal intubation, and link to a ventilator.
Inject anesthetic intraperitoneally.
Perform a tracheotomy and intubate mice for assisted ventilation.
Incise the chest with a thoracotomy of 0.5 cm–1 cm width on the left side around the 5th rib.
Re-section up to 3 ribs and stabilize using rib retractors.
Carefully move the left lung sideways to expose the heart.
Place window for imaging using a suction system linked to a ring holder for stabilization.
Create a vacuum with the ring holder to immobilize the thorax partially and stabilize it.
Use a round coverslip (#1.5, 15–20 mm diameter) to create an optical window on the heart surface via reversible vacuum pressure.
Place mouse in dorsal recumbency on a custom-built stage for full-body support.
Immobile limbs and tail should be secured with adhesive tape.
Introduce tubing for oxygenation and vacuum generation into the imaging setup.
Use an inverted microscope with at least a 63× objective positioned over the optical window site.
Confirm no significant vascular damage or blood flow alterations before acquiring images.
Place the mouse in dorsal recumbency for liver IVM procedure.
Locate the xiphoid process as the caudal thoracic limit reference point.
Perform a small horizontal surgical incision immediately below the xiphoid process.
Inject anesthetic intraperitoneally.
Make a small incision (up to 5 mm) at the site of the xiphoid process.
Eject either the middle or part of the left liver lobe using cotton buds.
Place a rectangular coverslip on the mouse and secure with surgical glue for inverted microscope imaging.
Attach a round coverslip to a vacuum ring and place it on top of the incision for upright microscope imaging.
Turn the mouse to display the ventral side for imaging in an inverted microscope setup.
Secure the mouse on the adjustable holder on the microscope stage for inverted microscope imaging.
Immobilize all limbs and tail of the mouse.
Add dyes intravenously before or after securing the mouse on the stage, based on experimental conditions.
Use forceps to lift the skin away from the liver.
Make a small cut on the skin.
Make a small horizontal cut in the abdominal muscles to reach the liver.
Identify liver lobes by their coloration (brownish/red).
Have a cauterizer ready for any major bleeding.
Ensure incisions are no more than 5 mm wide to prevent alterations to cardiac and respiratory output.
Carefully extend the incision as needed to expose the liver lobe.
Push the left liver lobe through the incision with moist cotton swabs.
Moisten the liver with saline solution (0.9% NaCl) or 1×PBS.
Place a window for imaging.
For a terminal window, add surgical glue above and below the incision.
Place a rectangular coverslip on top of the organ.
Use a suction system linked to a ring that acts as a holder for a glass slide to create a vacuum.
Allow the abdomen stabilization via 20–25 mmHg of reversible vacuum using a round coverslip (#1.5, 15–20 mm diameter).
Place mouse on stage and image.
Position the objective below the window on the surgical incision for an inverted microscope with a 63× or 100× oil immersion objectives.
Position the objective above the window on the surgical incision for an upright microscope with a 63× or 100× oil immersion objectives.
Confirm that no significant vascular damage or blood flow alterations occurred.
Acquire images as needed.
Place the mouse in right lateral recumbency for spleen IVM.
Inject anesthetic intraperitoneally.
Make a small incision (up to 5 mm) and carefully expose the spleen.
Use a rectangular coverslip and secure it on the mouse using surgical glue for option 1 imaging setup.
Attach a round coverslip with a vacuum ring directly over the incision for option 2 imaging setup.
Place the mouse on the microscope stage laterally for inverted microscope imaging (option 1).
Secure the coverslip attached to the mouse onto an adjustable holder for inverted microscope use.
Immobilize all limbs and tail of the mouse on the custom-built stage.
Insert tubing for vacuum and intravenous cannulation, as required by experimental conditions.
Add dyes intravenously before or after securing the mouse on the stage, based on experimental requirements.
Use forceps to lift the skin away from the spleen.
Make a small cut on the skin only and retract the skin to generate a small field of view.
Visualize the underlying spleen.
Locate a large ascending vessel once the muscle is exposed.
Perform a small diagonal incision near the large ascending vessel with care.
Ensure the incision on the skin and muscle does not exceed 5 mm in width.
Handle the spleen with great care to avoid bleeding.
Use blunt forceps carefully when handling the spleen.
Place the surgical incision to expose the pancreas and up to one-third of the spleen.
Ensure sufficient tissue exposure to prevent retraction into the body cavity.
Hydrate the exposed tissues with saline solution or 1×PBS.
Apply surgical glue above and below the surgical incision for a terminal window setup.
Place a coverslip on top of the organ after applying surgical glue.
Alternatively, use a suction system linked to a ring holder for partial immobilization of the spleen.
Create a vacuum using the suction system at 20–25 mmHg to stabilize the tissues.
Use a round coverslip (#1.5, 15-20 mm diameter) to create a window on the organ surface.
Allow loose adherence of the coverslip to the spleen surface via reversible vacuum pressure.
Place mouse on stage and image the spleen.
Position mouse in left lateral recumbency or right lateral recumbency on suitable microscope stage.
Use inverted microscope with 63× or 100× oil immersion objective for left lateral positioning.
Position objective below surgical incision for left lateral positioning.
Use upright microscopy with 63× or 100× oil immersion objective for right lateral positioning.
Position objective above surgical incision for right lateral positioning.
Confirm no significant vascular damage occurred.
Acquire images as needed.
Inject anesthetic intraperitoneally.
Make a small incision up to 5 mm to expose the pancreas.
Place a rectangular coverslip on the mouse using surgical glue for inverted microscope imaging.
Attach a round coverslip with a vacuum ring on top of the incision for upright microscope imaging.
Turn the mouse laterally and secure it on an adjustable holder for inverted microscope imaging.
Provide full body support to the mouse on a custom-built stage for older mice using upright microscope imaging.
Use forceps to lift the skin away from the pancreas.
Make a small cut on the skin only.
Retract the skin to generate a small field of view.
Visualize the underlying pancreas.
Locate a large ascending vessel in the exposed muscle.
Perform a small diagonal incision near but avoiding the large vessel.
Ensure that the incision is no more than 5 mm wide.
Place a window for imaging.
Expose the pancreas and ensure enough tissue is visible to prevent retraction into the body.
Avoid injuring blood and lymphatic vasculature during surgery.
Hydrate the organ with saline solution (0.9% NaCl) or 1×PBS.
Add surgical glue above and below the surgical incision for a terminal window.
Place a coverslip on top of the organ.
Inject anesthetic intraperitoneally.
Make a small incision up to 5 mm to expose the kidney.
Place a rectangular coverslip on the mouse using surgical glue for imaging with an inverted microscope.
Attach a round coverslip to a vacuum ring and place it on top of the incision for imaging with an upright microscope.
Turn the mouse laterally to display the left or right side for imaging in an inverted microscope setup.
Secure the coverslip attached to the mouse on an adjustable holder on the microscope stage for younger mice.
Provide full body support to older mice using a custom-built stage and allow space for tubing.
Immobobilize all limbs and tail of the mouse during imaging.
Use forceps to lift the skin away from the kidney.
Make a small cut on the skin to retract it and generate a small field of view.
Visualize the underlying kidney under the muscle layer.
Have a cauterizer ready to address any major bleeding.
Ensure the incision on the skin and muscle is no more than 5 mm in width.
Place a window for imaging carefully.
Gently retract the surgical incision to expose the dorsal side of the kidney.
Hydrate the organ with saline solution (0.9% NaCl) or 1×PBS.
For a terminal window, add surgical glue above and below the surgical incision.
Place a coverslip on top of the organ.
Place mouse on stage and image.
Position the objective below the window on the surgical incision for window option 1 using an inverted microscope with a 63× or 100× oil immersion objectives.
Position the objective above the window on the surgical incision for window option 2 using an upright microscopy with a 63× or 100× oil immersion objectives.
Prepare suitable stages or holders for positioning the mouse within the microscope.
Place the mouse in ventral recumbency.
Lift the skin away from the mid-calf using forceps.
Cut the skin vertically up to the upper thigh.
Inject anesthetic intraperitoneally.
Make a small incision on one of the lower limbs (up to 2 mm).
Carefully move subcutaneous adipose tissues and muscles to expose the popliteal lymph node.
Hydrate the site of incision for direct imaging.
Use a round coverslip attached to a vacuum ring and place it on top of the incision if required.
Generate skin flaps by making two horizontal skin incisions at the top of the vertical incision line.
Separate the skin as needed to expose the lymph node.
Separate the lymph node from surrounding adipose and muscle tissues carefully.
Hydrate the separated lymph node with warm saline solution or 1×PBS.
Place a window for imaging on the hydrated lymph node.
Secure a glass coverslip onto the tissue using surgical glue or suction.
Position the mouse on the microscope stage for imaging.
Use an upright microscope equipped with a 63× or 100× oil immersion objective lens.
Place the objective below the window on the surgical incision site.
Confirm no significant vascular damage has occurred during surgery.
Acquire images as needed to document any blood flow alterations.
Locate the site of interest in the pelvis, on either lateral location, at the level of the upper thigh and before the knee.
Prepare the surgical site as necessary.
Inject anesthetic intraperitoneally.
Make a small incision in the pelvis, lateral to the area of the knee (up to 5 mm).
Carefully expose the g-WAT.
Place a rectangular coverslip over the exposed g-WAT using surgical glue for imaging with an inverted microscope.
Secure the mouse on an adjustable holder on the microscope stage for ventral side imaging.
Attach a round coverslip to a vacuum ring and place it on top of the incision for upright microscope imaging.
Provide full body support to the mouse on a custom-built stage allowing space for tubing used for vacuum and intravenous cannulation.
Use the forceps to lift the skin away from the pelvis.
Cut diagonally and downwards to expose the underlying muscle.
Locate the gonadal adipose tissue.
Make a small incision in the muscle and peritoneum to expose the gonadal adipose tissue.
Take care during surgery to avoid injuring the vasculature near the hind leg adipose tissue and muscle.
Make the surgical incision small within the confines of the pelvis to stabilize the organ adequately.
Place forceps inside the pelvis through the peritoneal incision.
Withdraw the full gonadal adipose tissue with care.
Avoid extending the adipose tissue too much to prevent damage to the vasculature and maintain tissue integrity.
Hydrate the withdrawn tissue with 1×PBS or saline solution (0.9% NaCl).
Create a window for imaging on the hydrated tissue.
Optionally, for a terminal window, apply surgical glue above and below the incision.
Place a coverslip over the organ after applying surgical glue.
Place mouse on stage and image using inverted microscope with 63× or 100× oil immersion objectives for window option 1.
Position objective below the window on the surgical incision for window option 1.
Place mouse in dorsal recumbency for window option 2.
Use upright microscopy with 63× or 100× oil immersion objectives for window option 2.
Position objective above the window on the surgical incision for window option 2.
Confirm no significant vascular damage occurred.
Acquire images as needed.
Remove 10-20 μl of blood from the tail vein of an unlabeled, uninfected mouse and collect in RPMI 1640.
Count the required number of RBCs using a Neubauer chamber or other method that enables quantification of RBC concentration.
Centrifuge cells at 800 g for 5 min.
Resuspend the pellet in 20 μM CFDA-SE or 10 μM DDAO-SE and incubate for 1 h at 37°C.
Wash the suspension with complete RPMI 1640 medium twice.
Resuspend in a final volume of 200 μL of 1× PBS.
Inject the full volume into an infected mouse ready for IVM imaging.
Choose a dye based on compatibility with other fluorescent reporters/markers used in the same assay.
Inject dyes and conjugated antibodies to visualize receptors or other markers of interest.
Inject conjugated antibodies for the vascular receptor of interest.
Resuspend Hoechst, 70 kDa FITC-Dextran, and A647-conjugated antibodies in 100-200 μL 1× PBS to achieve the desired concentration per mouse.
Inject the full volume into the mouse.
Determine perfusion kinetics based on the research requirements.
Begin imaging at a suitable time post-injection.
If necessary for research, immediately begin imaging after injection of FITC-Dextran.
(Optional) Surround the vessel or capillary of interest with sutures.
Tighten the sutures to completely or partially block blood flow.
Visualize T. brucei behavior within the vascular endothelium without blood flow.
Position the mouse on the imaging stage after successful surgery and labeling steps.
Image at least 30 fields of view per tissue per mouse for comprehensive coverage.
Ensure contiguous fields of view to minimize quantification biases.
Establish a method for continuous monitoring during imaging sessions.
For time-lapse imaging, define suitable total times and intervals based on research objectives.
Maintain the anesthetized state of the mouse throughout the entire imaging process.
Provide cardiac resuscitation if necessary during imaging procedures.
Euthanize the mouse using an anesthetic overdose and/or cervical dislocation while the mouse remains anesthetized.
Place mice cadavers in a freezer or dispose according to institute regulations.
